extracted.intended_audience: public commenters on federal regulations (especially OIRA-reviewed/significant rules); regulatory advocates, attorneys, and policy analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting public comments intended to influence OIRA-reviewed (significant) federal regulations, emphasizing plain language, clear requests, and engagement with cost–benefit analysis. Focuses on structuring comments so busy agency or OIRA staff can quickly grasp and act on the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak in plain English
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid jargon; if technical terms are necessary, define them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clear, everyday language so non-specialist agency or OIRA staff can understand the point. Define any necessary technical terms rather than assuming background knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the request unambiguous / specific
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the agency exactly what to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give a concrete, actionable instruction — e.g., propose specific regulatory text, a particular numeric standard, or an explicit procedural change — so the agency can implement the suggestion without guesswork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide readable summaries (lead with summary, follow with detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with a summary, follow with detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a concise executive summary stating the requested change and main reasons; put supporting evidence and technical detail later so readers can get the gist quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce cognitive burden / structure for navigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure the comment so a busy reader can navigate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use headings, numbered points, bullets, short paragraphs, and clear signaling so reviewers can find key claims, evidence, and suggestions quickly. Design the document for skim-reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use defaults wisely
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the rule sets defaults, propose better defaults.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify any default options in the proposed rule and explain why an alternative default would improve outcomes; quantify impacts when possible and explain behavioral implications of defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use disclosure to reduce opacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand or provide better disclosures where the rule is opaque.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose specific disclosure requirements or clearer presentation of information so affected parties and regulators can better understand costs, risks, or tradeoffs; include sample disclosure language if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use behavioral insights
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference behavioral economics where relevant to predicted responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting how individuals or firms will respond to the rule, cite behavioral-science evidence (nudges, defaults, heuristics) and explain how these mechanisms affect compliance, benefits, and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect to costs and benefits / frame to support CBA
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the comment to support the agency's cost–benefit analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie arguments to monetizable and non-monetizable benefits/costs as appropriate; show how the proposed change affects net benefits and the agency's regulatory impact analysis (RIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage with the agency's RIA directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective comments on significant rules engage with the agency's regulatory impact analysis (RIA) directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to specific sections, tables, or assumptions in the RIA; critique methods, inputs, or omissions; and show how the RIA should be revised in light of the commenter's evidence or proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify deficiencies in cost/benefit estimates with specific numbers
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify deficiencies in cost or benefit estimates with specific numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not only assert errors — provide corrected calculations, alternative data, or estimates (with sources) to show the magnitude and direction of the agency's mistakes or uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose alternatives with their own cost–benefit characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose alternatives and provide their cost–benefit consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When recommending a different regulatory design, include an estimate of its costs and benefits (or a reasoned qualitative comparison) so the agency can compare options within its CBA framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address behavioral assumptions in the agency's analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Address behavioral assumptions where relevant to the agency's analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scrutinize and, where warranted, challenge assumptions about how people behave under the rule; supply empirical evidence or studies that support alternative behavioral parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide plain-language summaries tailored to OIRA staff
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain-language summaries OIRA staff can quickly digest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare a short, high-value summary emphasizing the CBA implications and key numeric corrections so OIRA reviewers can rapidly assess the comment's relevance to the RIA and decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain readability even when challenging cost–benefit framing
rubrics_metrics.description: If the comment resists the cost–benefit framework (e.g., equity or dignity arguments), structure it for readability nonetheless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize normative or rights-based critiques clearly (summary first, clear claims, supporting evidence), so they are persuasive and accessible even if they do not fit the agency's dominant analytical approach.
